title: Strict mutations have no request-stable replay or duplicate-command guard
observed_behavior: Every accepted strict request receives a fresh server UUID, writes an accepted history entry, and dispatches the mutation. The journal record path only prepends and persists entries; it does not reserve a caller-stable identity, compare a fingerprint, report in-progress work, or replay a prior terminal result.
expected_invariant: Every strict mutation must be idempotent across concurrent delivery, lost-response retry, and process restart by using a validated request-stable command identity plus a canonical route/payload fingerprint; conflicting identity reuse must be rejected before mutation.
root_cause: Strict evidence was implemented as append-only audit history rather than an atomic command reservation and replay protocol, while command IDs are generated after receipt instead of supplied stably by the caller.
failure_scenario: A strict rename, publish, lifecycle, network, pipeline, audit, or rerun mutation succeeds but its HTTP response is lost, or two equivalent requests arrive concurrently. Each attempt receives a different UUID and reaches the facade mutation method, so side effects can execute more than once with no uniform handler-level replay result.
evidence: handler.py line 121 assigns uuid.uuid4().hex for every strict request and line 149 invokes the mutation after only an accepted journal append
CommandJournal.record lines 49-68 contains no identity lookup, reservation, fingerprint, or replay branch

repository search found X-MediaPipeline-Command-ID, strict_command_fingerprint, reserve_strict_command, and complete_strict_command only in tests/python/desktop/test_command_replay_adversarial.py and not in src/
read-only registry comparison confirmed the policy applies to 23 strict routes within 117 registered POST commands
supporting adversarial test sections at lines 193-298 and 434-472 specify concurrent duplicate, lost-response, restart replay, and cross-route conflict expectations that production does not implement
affected_flows: pipeline, audit, rerun, backend, and network lifecycle commands
existing_safeguards: Local API token and origin checks precede dispatch
route contracts enforce strict boolean confirmations
accepted evidence is persisted before mutation
some individual domain services have duplicate or active-process guards
safeguard_gap: Authorization and confirmation establish intent but do not make delivery idempotent. Domain-specific guards are neither uniform across all strict routes nor able to replay the original terminal HTTP result after a lost response.
tests_present: tests/python/desktop/test_application_facade_local_api_process_commands.py checks a fresh returned 32-hex command ID and accepted/terminal evidence
tests/python/desktop/test_command_replay_adversarial.py contains intended concurrent, restart, response-loss, and conflict cases but was supporting evidence only and was not executed in this slice

passing lost-response replay test returning the original terminal result without redispatch
restart replay and same-ID/different-route-or-payload conflict tests against the actual journal implementation
representative strict-route tests for rename, publish, lifecycle, network, pipeline, audit, and rerun domains
recommended_remediation: Accept and strictly validate a caller-stable idempotency/command ID, fingerprint the canonical route plus validated payload, and atomically reserve it in the authoritative command journal before dispatch. Return a defined in-progress response for an active reservation, replay the persisted terminal response for a completed match, reject identity/fingerprint conflicts, and define retention and crash recovery while preserving existing domain guards.
remediation_risk: High: introducing generic replay changes all strict mutation semantics and must avoid replaying stale authorization, leaking stored responses, treating different payloads as equivalent, or deadlocking abandoned reservations. Migrate journal schema and retention explicitly.
validation_rung: Targeted journal and handler unit tests plus concurrent HTTP, lost-response, restart, strict-JSON, command-journal, and affected Local API smokes; exercise representative high-risk mutation routes with synthetic fixtures and no real source-media mutation.
prior_audit_relationship: not reconciled; no current-hash completion or disposition was inherited from the prior audit

title: Mutation exceptions leave accepted strict commands without durable terminal or indeterminate evidence
observed_behavior: Strict terminal evidence is written only after a mutation returns normally. A dispatch exception reaches generic route-exception journaling, where request._command_id preserves correlation to the accepted command, but the entry has no canonical evidence_phase or journal_durability and is written best-effort rather than through strict persistence.
expected_invariant: Every durably accepted strict command must acquire a linked durable terminal state or an explicit indeterminate recovery marker before the server responds or permits a retry, including when command implementation raises after possible side effects.
root_cause: The strict command state machine covers normal return and terminal-journal-write failure but does not own exceptions thrown by mutation dispatch. The generic exception path retains nested request-level ID correlation yet cannot establish a durable failed or indeterminate terminal state.
failure_scenario: A facade method mutates filesystem, process, queue, rename, publish, or lifecycle state and then raises. History may contain an accepted entry plus a correlatable generic 500 without a durable terminal phase; if the generic write also fails, only the accepted entry remains. After restart, the operator and any replay layer cannot determine whether retrying is safe.
evidence: handler.py line 149 performs mutation dispatch before the normal-return terminal evidence block at lines 150-169
handler.py lines 171-179 catch dispatch exceptions through generic route-exception journaling without strict=True or the indeterminate-marker adapter

handler.py line 148 injects _command_id into the validated request and line 176 passes that body to generic journaling; an independent temporary HTTP probe confirmed request._command_id equals the accepted command ID
handler_policy.py route_exception_journal_payload lines 127-155 has no evidence_phase, journal_durability, or canonical top-level command_id
the current passing process-command test asserts the accepted-plus-generic-exception shape but not a durable failed or indeterminate lifecycle state
when terminal strict-journal persistence fails after a successful mutation, handler.py lines 152-168 sends an indeterminate 503 without proving the optional marker became durable
server.py lines 233-246 can return after logging when no lifecycle state root exists or marker persistence fails; an adversarial temporary test then retried and performed a second mutation
affected_flows: every strict mutation whose implementation can partially apply before raising
rename, pending-publish, completed repair, and final promotion
existing_safeguards: accepted evidence records intent before dispatch
generic exception response hides internal exception text behind an error ID
generic exception journal evidence is bounded and redacted
normal-return terminal persistence failure returns 503 and attempts an indeterminate marker
safeguard_gap: Nested request correlation identifies which accepted command saw the route exception, but the generic entry cannot state whether side effects occurred and is not a strict durable terminal state. The separate terminal-write failure path can also claim indeterminate status without proof that its optional recovery marker persisted.
tests_present: tests/python/desktop/test_application_facade_local_api_process_commands.py verifies the current accepted-plus-correlatable-generic-exception shape
tests/python/desktop/test_api_handler_policy.py verifies bounded route exception payload helpers and journal eligibility

fault-injection test where a strict facade method raises after a synthetic side effect and records durable indeterminate recovery evidence

restart recovery-status test that prevents unsafe retry until the accepted command is reconciled
recommended_remediation: Retain strict command context around dispatch and handle command exceptions inside that state machine. Record linked failed terminal evidence only when non-application is proven; otherwise require a durable indeterminate lease/recovery marker before responding. Treat marker absence or persistence failure as an explicit unresolved evidence fault, and prevent replay until reconciliation proves the prior outcome.
remediation_risk: High: misclassifying a partially applied command as failed could authorize destructive replay, while marking every pre-side-effect validation/runtime exception indeterminate could unnecessarily block operators. Command implementations may need explicit side-effect boundary signals.
validation_rung: Targeted handler/policy unit tests, HTTP fault injection immediately before and after a synthetic side effect, restart/recovery-status checks, strict JSON and command journal tests, and affected Local API smokes.

title: Malformed command history is treated as empty and can be overwritten while health reports clean
observed_behavior: Malformed JSON or an unreadable journal is logged and replaced in memory with an empty list without retaining a load-error state. Persistence health therefore reports JSON status not_attempted and degraded false, and the next record atomically replaces the original path with the new truncated history.
expected_invariant: Unreadable authoritative command evidence must be preserved, surfaced as degraded, and cause strict mutations to fail closed until explicit recovery establishes authority; startup must never silently convert corruption into an apparently healthy empty history.
root_cause: Load failures are handled as an empty-history convenience path, while persistence health tracks only save-time and SQLite-mirror errors. Atomic save then treats the empty replacement state as authoritative.
failure_scenario: A crash, partial external write, disk error, or malformed journal exists at Local API startup. The server reports clean persistence, accepts a strict mutation, and replaces evidence containing a prior accepted or terminal record, destroying the information needed to decide whether a retry is safe.
evidence: CommandJournal._load lines 125-134 catches JSONDecodeError and OSError, logs a warning, and returns []
CommandJournal.to_mapping lines 70-89 derives degraded state from _last_json_save_error and _last_sqlite_error only, so load corruption is absent
CommandJournal._save_locked lines 136-174 serializes current in-memory entries and replaces the journal path
existing tests cover valid reload, save failure, SQLite failure, and temp cleanup but no malformed startup followed by strict mutation
test_command_replay_adversarial.py lines 400-432 specifies fail-closed malformed-history and degraded-status expectations that the production state fields cannot satisfy
affected_flows: Local API startup and /api/commands persistence health
all strict command acceptance after corrupted history
operator incident reconstruction and restart recovery
JSON authority and opportunistic SQLite mirror reconciliation
existing_safeguards: ordinary saves use same-directory temporary files, flush, fsync, and atomic replace
strict save-time JSON failures raise and roll back the new in-memory entry
SQLite mirror failure is reported as degraded without replacing JSON authority
a warning is emitted when load fails
safeguard_gap: Atomic replacement protects a valid write but cannot protect evidence already discarded during load. A log warning is not represented in operator-visible persistence health and does not stop mutation or preserve the corrupt original.

recommended_remediation: Retain a durable journal-load error state, preserve or quarantine the unreadable file without overwriting it, expose degraded authority in /api/commands and health surfaces, and block strict mutations until an explicit recovery path validates or restores command history. Define whether a verified SQLite copy may assist recovery without silently changing authority.
remediation_risk: Medium-high: fail-closed startup can block operator commands during disk incidents, while automatic salvage can misorder or omit command evidence. Recovery must preserve originals, make authority explicit, and avoid treating the best-effort mirror as authoritative without validation.
validation_rung: Corrupt, truncated, invalid-shape, and permission-denied startup unit tests; strict mutation fail-closed HTTP tests; backup/quarantine and recovery tests; persistence-health assertions; and command-history Local API smokes.

title: Depth limiting can persist sensitive mapping values in plaintext
observed_behavior: At depth four, bounded_command_evidence stringifies the entire value before checking whether it is a mapping with sensitive keys. The downstream text redactor handles URLs, key=value assignments, and bearer headers but not Python/JSON mapping syntax, so a nested password value survives into persistable evidence.
expected_invariant: No command request, result, error, or loaded-history path may persist credential material, regardless of nesting depth, truncation boundary, container type, or string representation.
root_cause: The recursion-depth guard runs before container and sensitive-key inspection and uses generic string conversion as truncation, converting structured secret-bearing data into opaque text that key-aware redaction no longer recognizes.
failure_scenario: A validated request, backend result, or loaded legacy entry contains password, token, join_blob, secret, api_key, or authorization data in a mapping at the recursion cap, possibly inside a list. The plaintext value is embedded in a string and written to local_api_command_history.json and the SQLite evidence mirror.
evidence: command_journal_policy.py lines 75-76 return _bounded_text(value) at depth >= 4 before the mapping branch at lines 77-84
core/network/url_policy.py lines 41-52 redacts URL credentials, key=value assignments, and bearer text but has no mapping-literal colon-value pattern
a bundled-Python probe with {'a': {'b': {'c': {'d': {'password': 'AUDIT_FAKE_SECRET_7e2'}}}}} returned a nested string containing the complete fake secret and printed FAKE_SECRET_PRESENT=True
current tests prove shallow key redaction but do not exercise a mapping at the cap

an independent temporary /api/settings/reload probe used only a synthetic fake secret; the extra=allow payload preserved the nested mapping through validation, bounded evidence, JSON persistence, and reload
the persisted and reloaded value contained {'password': 'AUDIT_FAKE_SECRET_W01_SR_4D91'} as plaintext at the depth cap
affected_flows: all Local API command journal request and result evidence
existing_safeguards: known sensitive mapping keys are replaced with <redacted> at shallower depths
scalar strings pass through network URL, assignment, and bearer redaction
evidence string/list/map sizes and history counts are bounded
secret-transfer validation failures can suppress request journaling
safeguard_gap: Depth truncation bypasses structured inspection precisely when content becomes opaque. Successful route results and loaded entries are not covered by validation-failure suppression, and bounded length limits exposure size rather than eliminating credentials.
tests_present: tests/python/desktop/test_api_command_journal_policy.py covers root and shallow nested sensitive keys, long values, lists, and loaded entries

recommended_remediation: Inspect mapping keys before enforcing the depth cap and replace over-depth containers with a constant truncation sentinel or a bounded key-aware shape; never call str or repr on an uninspected container. Apply equivalent defensive handling when sanitizing loaded legacy entries and consider rejecting already stringified credential-shaped mappings.
remediation_risk: Low-medium: changing evidence shape may affect diagnostics and snapshots, and overaggressive text patterns can redact benign data. Preserve schema compatibility and test useful nonsecret evidence at the boundary.
validation_rung: Focused journal-policy tests across depths 3-6, mappings nested in lists, every sensitive alias, long URL/bearer/assignment forms, loaded-entry sanitation, and persisted JSON/SQLite absence checks using only synthetic fake secrets.

title: Backend shutdown reports success when its callback was never scheduled
observed_behavior: The shutdown helper catches a Timer construction/start failure, logs it, and returns no status. The caller then returns ok=true with 'Backend shutdown requested' even though no callback can run and the backend remains alive.
expected_invariant: A lifecycle command must not acknowledge a shutdown request as accepted when the only scheduling attempt failed synchronously before the response was built.
root_cause: _request_backend_shutdown_after_response suppresses scheduling exceptions without returning success/failure, so _backend_shutdown_payload cannot distinguish a scheduled callback from a logged no-op.
failure_scenario: Thread/timer creation fails during resource exhaustion, interpreter shutdown, or an adapter fault. The shell receives a successful shutdown result and may proceed as though backend ownership is ending, while the process continues serving with no queued shutdown callback.
evidence: commands_process.py lines 78-83 catch every Timer construction/start exception and only log it
commands_process.py lines 372-378 unconditionally return backend_shutdown_success_payload after calling the helper
an in-memory probe patched threading.Timer.start to raise; production logged the traceback but returned ok=true and message 'Backend shutdown requested'
the existing lifecycle test explicitly verifies only that timer-start failure is logged and does not assert a truthful command result
affected_flows: Tauri/native close and backend ownership handoff
existing_safeguards: shutdown is blocked when close-readiness is unsafe unless forced cleanup is confirmed
synchronous timer failures and asynchronous callback failures are logged with tracebacks
normal scheduled shutdown uses a daemon timer after the HTTP response
safeguard_gap: Logging is not part of the command response or durable lifecycle evidence. A synchronous scheduling failure is knowable before returning and should not be represented as accepted shutdown.
tests_present: tests/python/desktop/test_application_facade_local_api_lifecycle.py covers safe/unsafe close readiness, forced cleanup, callback exceptions, and timer-start logging
tests_missing: HTTP or mixin test asserting timer construction/start failure returns ok=false and keeps lifecycle ownership explicit
durable command-journal assertion for a shutdown scheduling failure

recommended_remediation: Make the scheduling helper return an explicit result (or raise a bounded lifecycle error) and return a non-success command payload when Timer construction/start fails. Preserve the error log and ensure the shell keeps backend ownership until a later successful request or explicit reconciliation.
remediation_risk: Medium: the HTTP response must still flush before a successful callback stops the server, and changing lifecycle timing can affect native close behavior. Validate both success timing and failure retry semantics.
validation_rung: Focused lifecycle mixin and HTTP tests with Timer constructor/start fault injection, command-journal outcome assertions, close-readiness checks, and affected Tauri backend open/close smoke. No real-media validation is required.
prior_audit_relationship: New current-hash finding. W01-002 covers durable evidence after mutation dispatch; this finding is distinct because the shutdown scheduling failure occurs synchronously after a successful lifecycle decision and is falsely acknowledged as accepted.

title: One nonnumeric cached channel value aborts the entire folder override preview
observed_behavior: Folder preview accepts queue snapshot rows as unvalidated mappings, then converts each cached audio channel value with int(...) without a safe fallback. A legacy or malformed value such as 'six' raises ValueError and escapes the preview route instead of producing partial metadata with a warning.
expected_invariant: A read-only advisory preview over cached state must isolate malformed row fields, retain the rest of the preview, and report degraded/partial evidence rather than fail the whole request.
root_cause: The snapshot loader validates only the outer object/list shape, while the audio normalizer assumes channels is integer-coercible and lacks the safe conversion used by neighboring metadata helpers.
failure_scenario: A legacy queue snapshot, partially written producer payload, or external diagnostic edit leaves one audio stream with a nonnumeric channels value. Any folder preview sampling that row raises, yielding a generic Local API route exception and hiding every other known file/conflict in the folder.
evidence: folder_preview.py lines 280-286 parse arbitrary JSON mapping rows without validating nested track fields
folder_preview.py line 381 calls int(row.get('channels') or 0) outside a try/except

tests_missing: nonnumeric, negative, null, and oversized cached channel values

title: A snapshot refresh thread-start failure permanently wedges the refresh gate
observed_behavior: _schedule_snapshot_refresh acquires the nonblocking coalescing lock, assigns a Thread object, and calls start without an exception cleanup path. If Thread construction or start fails synchronously, the exception escapes while the lock remains held, so every later snapshot read skips scheduling and can show initializing or stale refresh-pending evidence forever.
expected_invariant: A synchronous failure to create or start a background status refresh must release the coalescing gate, clear the unusable thread slot, record the failure, and allow a later request to retry.
root_cause: The lock is released only in _refresh_snapshot_cache.finally, which can run only after a thread starts; there is no try/except around Thread construction and start in the scheduling method.
failure_scenario: During temporary thread/resource exhaustion or an injected adapter failure, an initial server start or later expired-cache read cannot start the refresh worker. The HTTP server can remain live, but status stays initializing or stale and no later request can recover without restarting the backend.
evidence: server.py lines 265-270 acquire _snapshot_refresh_lock and call thread.start without synchronous cleanup
server.py lines 272-301 release the lock only inside the worker target
a no-write in-memory BrokenThread probe made start raise, then reported lock_available_after_failure=False and left _snapshot_refresh_thread set to the unusable object
existing HTTP tests cover successful background refresh, coalescing while the lock is held, and provider exceptions after a worker starts, but not thread construction/start failure
affected_flows: GET routes that consume the cached snapshot
dashboard status liveness after transient thread exhaustion
existing_safeguards: a nonblocking lock coalesces normal concurrent refresh requests
_refresh_snapshot_cache catches provider exceptions, records a readable error, and releases the lock in finally
snapshot reads return a bounded initializing or stale projection instead of blocking
safeguard_gap: All safeguards assume the worker target begins executing. A failure before the target starts bypasses the only lock release and error-state update.
tests_present: tests/python/desktop/test_application_facade_local_api_http.py covers successful asynchronous initialization, one-worker coalescing, an externally held gate, and snapshot-provider exceptions
tests_missing: Thread constructor failure releases the gate and permits a second scheduling attempt
Thread.start failure clears the slot and produces readable refresh-failure evidence
LocalApiServer.start cleans up the already-started HTTP server if initial refresh scheduling fails
recommended_remediation: Wrap Thread construction/start in try/except, clear _snapshot_refresh_thread, record a bounded refresh error, and release the acquired lock before re-raising or returning. If start() treats this as fatal, also shut down the HTTP server/thread it already created; otherwise prove a later request retries successfully.
remediation_risk: Low-medium: lock ownership must remain single-release across both the scheduling and worker paths, and start failure policy must not strand a serving backend. Exercise normal success, concurrent coalescing, provider failure, and injected constructor/start failures.
validation_rung: Focused LocalApiServer unit/HTTP tests with synthetic Thread constructor and start faults plus normal snapshot cache/coalescing tests. No real-media validation is required.
prior_audit_relationship: New current-hash finding. W01-005 also concerns synchronous background scheduling failure, but that finding covers a falsely successful shutdown command; this finding covers a separately locked snapshot-refresh retry gate.

title: CSV rerun metadata augmentation can destroy valid terminal worker evidence and force a retry
observed_behavior: After validating a successful local_worker_result.v1 artifact, the provider augments CSV-rerun metadata by calling Path.write_text directly on the same terminal evidence file. A partial write failure truncates or corrupts the only valid artifact; the catch then discards the already validated result and the done projection marks the job failed_result_invalid with retry_on_failure=true.
expected_invariant: Backend-authored terminal worker evidence must never be destructively rewritten in place. Metadata enrichment must be atomic or separate, and an enrichment failure must not convert a proven successful process/result into retryable missing evidence.
root_cause: The enrichment path overwrites the authoritative artifact with a non-atomic open/truncate/write operation, and its error policy treats augmentation failure as failure of the underlying validated worker result.
failure_scenario: A CSV rerun encode exits zero and writes a valid success artifact and handoff output. Disk exhaustion, interruption, antivirus interference, or an injected write failure occurs during coordinator-metadata enrichment. The artifact is left partial, the coordinator receives a retryable failure, and the already completed source can be claimed and processed again while the original handoff output still exists.
evidence: network_lifecycle_provider.py lines 159-186 fully validate schema, claim/run identity, booleans, and integer fields before augmentation
lines 187-192 call result_path.write_text on the validated artifact and return no result on any write error
lines 210-223 convert that enrichment error to success=false, failed_result_invalid, queue_terminal=false, and retry_on_failure=true
a temporary synthetic valid success artifact plus a patched partial write reproduced returned_result_is_none=True and left the artifact as the single byte '{'
the full done-projection probe returned success=false, completion_status=failed_result_invalid, retry_on_failure=true after a zero process return code
affected_flows: coordinator done reporting and retry scheduling
existing_safeguards: the artifact is validated before enrichment
claim ID and run ID must match the active job
field types and nonnegative counters are checked
write exceptions are caught and redacted before reporting
safeguard_gap: Validation protects what is read but not the subsequent destructive rewrite. Catching the exception does not restore the original bytes or preserve its already established success semantics.
tests_present: tests/python/desktop/test_application_facade_network_lifecycle.py covers ordinary valid worker results, missing/invalid result shapes, claim/run identity mismatch, and scalar type rejection
tests_missing: partial enrichment write preserves the original valid artifact byte-for-byte
atomic temp/replace failure retains prior evidence and reports enrichment separately
successful output is not made retryable solely because optional metadata persistence failed
restart recovery after interruption between metadata temp write and replace
recommended_remediation: Build and validate the augmented payload in memory, write it to a sibling temporary file, fsync as appropriate, and atomically replace only after a complete successful write; preserve or back up the original. Prefer a separate coordinator-metadata sidecar when worker evidence should remain immutable. If optional enrichment fails, report that failure without reclassifying the validated underlying success as retryable.
remediation_risk: Medium-high: worker result status drives claim completion, retries, and output handoff. Preserve schema/identity checks and prove retry policy, collision handling, restart recovery, and artifact immutability under injected partial-write failures.
validation_rung: Focused network lifecycle and CSV rerun tests with temporary synthetic result files, write/replace fault injection, coordinator done/retry assertions, and restart recovery. No representative real-media validation is required for the write-transaction defect itself.
prior_audit_relationship: New current-hash finding; no current exact-location finding on this provider described destructive post-validation result enrichment.

title: Startup timing registry retains every completed steps list indefinitely
observed_behavior: Every call with a new steps list inserts that list into the module-global _STARTUP_TIMERS mapping. There is no removal path after startup completes, so the mapping holds a strong reference to each list and all nested step payloads for the lifetime of the Python process.
expected_invariant: Transient startup timing state should be scoped to one startup operation and released when that operation completes, rather than accumulating globally across repeated backend construction or direct helper use.
root_cause: Timing state is keyed by id(steps) in a process-global dictionary, but the dictionary value retains the steps object itself and no caller or final startup step evicts the entry.
failure_scenario: Tests, embedded callers, restart-in-process flows, or repeated build_backend attempts create fresh startup-step lists. Each attempt permanently grows _STARTUP_TIMERS and retains every diagnostic payload reachable from the list; long-lived processes can accumulate unbounded memory.
evidence: local_api_main.py line 35 declares a process-global dict whose values contain the full steps list
record_startup_step lines 147-152 reads and then unconditionally stores the list without any corresponding pop or cleanup
repository-wide search found no other _STARTUP_TIMERS references and therefore no eviction path

an isolated bundled-Python probe created 200 fresh lists, deleted the local reference, forced garbage collection, and observed baseline=0, after=200, retained=200 with every list still strongly referenced
affected_flows: tests or integrations calling record_startup_step with fresh lists
existing_safeguards: The normal packaged process generally constructs the backend only once
The retained payloads are diagnostic dictionaries rather than source-media data
safeguard_gap: Single-start assumptions limit typical growth but do not enforce bounded state, and build failures or embedded/test reuse can execute the helper repeatedly in one process.
tests_missing: A repeated-build or helper-level test asserting timer state is released after startup completion
A regression test proving timing continuity without a global strong-reference registry
recommended_remediation: Carry timing state in an explicit startup context object or attach only scalar timing metadata to the active list lifecycle, and remove the registry entry in a guaranteed completion/failure cleanup path. Add a bounded-state regression test.
remediation_risk: Low to medium: changing timing ownership must preserve elapsed/duration values across copied startup-step lists and callback emission.
validation_rung: Targeted unit tests for record_startup_step and build_backend startup progress, including repeated construction and failure cleanup; no real media fixture is required.
prior_audit_relationship: not reconciled; no current-hash finding at this location was present in the assembled or worker finding ledgers

title: Future-dated signed requests become replayable after nonce eviction
observed_behavior: A valid request timestamped at the positive edge of the allowed clock-skew window is accepted and its nonce expires at receipt_time + max_skew. Immediately after that eviction, the same timestamp is still valid for nearly another max_skew interval, so the identical captured request is accepted again.
expected_invariant: A nonce must remain unavailable for at least the entire period during which its signed timestamp can pass validation, so one valid HMAC request can be accepted at most once.
root_cause: Nonce expiry is calculated from the coordinator's receipt time (`current + max_skew_seconds`) rather than the signed timestamp's latest-valid horizon (or a conservative two-skew retention window).
failure_scenario: Because coordinator traffic is plain HTTP on the LAN, an observer captures a future-skewed signed claim, done, release, registration, or other mutation request. After five minutes the nonce entry is removed while the signature remains timestamp-valid; replay can allocate another job, repeat lifecycle state changes, or otherwise mutate coordinator state a second time.
evidence: auth.py lines 213-214 accepts timestamps within absolute skew
auth.py lines 215-221 removes nonces at receipt_time + skew and then inserts the nonce with that same horizon

a deterministic bundled-Python probe used timestamp=1300, first receipt now=1000, max_skew=300; the request was accepted, nonce expiry became 1300, and the identical request replayed at now=1301 was accepted again with expiry 1601
affected_flows: worker registration and coordinator state mutations
existing_safeguards: HMAC-SHA256 binds method, exact path/query, timestamp, nonce, and body
signatures are constant-time compared

title: Abort callback failure leaves reclaimed worker media processing alive without heartbeats
observed_behavior: When a reclaim or prolonged heartbeat failure requires abort, the worker schedules an app callback and immediately exits the heartbeat loop. title: FiredRegistry access reordering can suppress events beyond the configured TTL
observed_behavior: Expiration stops at the first non-expired OrderedDict entry, assuming timestamp order. `has_fired` moves a hit to the end without refreshing its stored timestamp, breaking that order; an expired entry behind a newer one is retained and continues suppressing the event.
expected_invariant: Every fired entry older than `ttl_seconds` must stop suppressing detections regardless of access order or other registry entries.
root_cause: The data structure combines LRU reordering with an expiration algorithm that is only correct for insertion/timestamp ordering.
failure_scenario: Path A fires at t=0 and B at t=5. Accessing A at t=6 moves its old timestamp behind B. At t=11 A is older than the 10-second TTL, but expiration sees unexpired B first and breaks, so A remains suppressed; continual newer entries can extend suppression far beyond TTL.

tests_missing: multiple paths with LRU reorder before expiry

recommended_remediation: Either refresh the timestamp when moving a hit (true sliding TTL), scan/delete all expired entries, or maintain separate timestamp-ordered expiry and LRU structures; document the intended TTL semantics.
